newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FORECAST - Malaysia growth seen slowing further in '97.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Malaysia growth seen slowing further in '97.

text.p: Malaysia's economic growth will slow in 1997, but strong money supply and a booming domestic market could trigger a resurgence in the worrisome current account deficit, economists said on Monday.
In a Reuters poll of Malaysian economic indicators, the economists said gross domestic product (GDP) growth would be about eight percent, in line with the government's forecast.
The poll of economists at 16 large research houses forecast an average GDP growth of 7.99 percent in 1997 against the government's projection of eight percent.
They forecast the 1996 GDP growth to average 8.08 percent against an official projection of 8.2 percent -- down from the 9.5 percent growth recorded in 1995.
Ten of those polled also provided predictions for the fourth quarter of 1996 and first quarter of 1997.
They forecast an average GDP growth of 7.91 percent in the fourth quarter of this year, against eight percent recorded in the third quarter and 9.2 percent in the fourth quarter of 1995.
In the first quarter of 1997, the economists projected growth at 8.01 percent, against 8.3 percent in the corresponding period of 1996.
Lower government spending and a downturn in the electronics sector were among the factors that moderated growth, they said.
"The forecasts are not that surprising. More and more they tend to gravitate towards the government's numbers," said Liew Yin Sze, an economist with J.M. Sassoon & Co in Singapore.
"People who were comparing Malaysia with Mexico last year will not have much to say after such good figures," he said.
A high current account deficit last year forced Mexico to devalue its currency, triggering an international crisis. Many had feared a similar meltdown in Malaysia.
Economists said Malaysia's current account gap was expected to be five percent of GDP this year, against nearly nine percent last year.
They forecast an average current account gap of 13.67 billion ringgit in 1996 and 13.03 billion in 1997, against the government's forecasts of 14.77 billion and 11.5 billion, respectively.
"But, I cannot be sure the current account will continue to improve," Liew Yin Sze said.

An economist with another research house said while Malaysia's economy was headed towards a soft landing, consumer spending remained strong. "That will pose some challenges to (central) Bank Negara's monetary management."
The research houses polled forecast that the benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur interbank offered rate (KLIBOR) will fall to 6.9 percent by the end of 1997 from 7.39 on Monday.
However, the decline would be gradual, with the three-month KLIBOR at an average 7.21 percent at the end of the first quarter of 1997, the Reuters poll said.
Credit growth, indicated by strong money supply, suggested consumer spending had not abated and interest rates should remain firm in the medium term, the economists said.
But they predicted a slowdown in money supply.

Money, as defined by M2 (money in circulation and cash on deposit in banks plus time, savings and foreign currency deposits), would grow by 18.9 percent year-on-year in 1996 and 17 percent in 1997, the poll found.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230 8911)
